title: II. Smerdyakov With A Guitar
paragraphs: He really had no time to lose. Even while saying goodbye to Lise, it had struck him that he needed to come up with some kind of scheme to track down his brother Dmitri, who was clearly avoiding him. It was getting late, nearly three o'clock. Alyosha's whole soul was pulling him back to the monastery, to his dying saint, but the need to see Dmitri outweighed everything else. The conviction that some great, unavoidable catastrophe was about to happen grew stronger in Alyosha's mind with every passing hour. What exactly that catastrophe would be, and what he would say to his brother at that moment, he probably couldn't have said with any certainty. "Even if my benefactor has to die without me there, at least I won't have to spend the rest of my life reproaching myself with the thought that I might have saved something and didn't—that I walked past and hurried home instead. If I do what I mean to do now, I'll be following his great teaching."

His plan was to catch his brother Dmitri unawares—to climb over the fence, as he had the day before, slip into the garden, and sit in the summer house. If Dmitri wasn't there, Alyosha thought, he wouldn't announce himself to Foma or the women of the house, but would stay hidden in the summer house, even if it meant waiting there until evening. If, as before, Dmitri were lying in wait for Grushenka to show up, he'd very likely come to the summer house himself. Alyosha didn't dwell much on the details of his plan, though; he simply resolved to act on it, even if it meant not getting back to the monastery that day.

Everything went smoothly; he climbed over the fence almost at the exact spot as the day before, and slipped into the summer house unseen. He didn't want to be noticed. The woman of the house, and Foma too, if he was around, might well be loyal to his brother and follow his instructions, refusing to let Alyosha into the garden, or might warn Dmitri that someone was looking for him.

There was no one in the summer house. Alyosha sat down and began to wait. He looked around the summer house, which somehow struck him as much older than it had seemed the day before. Though the day was every bit as fine as yesterday, this time the place seemed a shabby little spot. There was a ring on the table, no doubt left by the glass of brandy spilled the day before. Foolish, irrelevant thoughts drifted through his mind, as they always do during a tedious wait. He found himself wondering, for instance, why he'd sat down in exactly the same spot as before, rather than somewhere else. At last he began to feel quite low—weighed down by suspense and uncertainty. But he hadn't been sitting there more than a quarter of an hour when he suddenly heard the strum of a guitar somewhere close by. People were sitting, or had just sat down, in the bushes no more than twenty paces off. Alyosha suddenly remembered that on his way out of the summer house the day before, he'd caught a glimpse of an old, low, green garden bench among the bushes to the left, by the fence. The people must be sitting there now. Who were they?
A man's voice suddenly started singing in a sugary falsetto, accompanying himself on the guitar:
With a force no one can master I am bound fast to my dear. O Lord, have mercy On her and on me! On her and on me! On her and on me!
The voice stopped. It was a lackey's tenor, and a lackey's song. Another voice, a woman's, asked suddenly, coyly and insinuatingly, with a kind of prim affectation:
"Why haven't you come to see us in so long, Pavel Fyodorovitch? Why do you always look down on us?"

"Not at all," a man's voice answered politely, but with pointed dignity. It was clear the man had the upper hand here, and that the woman was the one making advances. "That must be Smerdyakov," Alyosha thought, "going by the voice. And the lady must be the daughter of the house, the one who came back from Moscow, who wears the dress with a train and goes to Marfa for her soup."
"I'm terribly fond of verses of all kinds, as long as they rhyme," the woman's voice went on. "Why don't you go on?"
The man sang again:
What do I care for royal treasure If my dear one's well, at leisure? Lord have mercy On her and on me! On her and on me! On her and on me!
"It sounded even better last time," the woman's voice observed. "You sang 'If my darling's well and gay'—it sounded more tender. I suppose you've forgotten it today."
"Poetry is rubbish!" Smerdyakov said curtly.
"Oh, no! I'm very fond of poetry."

"As far as it's poetry, it's essentially rubbish. Think about it yourself—who ever actually talks in rhyme? And if we all had to talk in rhyme, even if the government decreed it, we wouldn't get much said, would we? Poetry's no good, Marya Kondratyevna."
"How clever you are! However did you come to think so deeply about everything?" The woman's voice grew more and more coaxing.

"I could have done far better than this. I could have known a great deal more than I do, if it weren't for my fate ever since childhood. I would have shot a man in a duel if he'd insulted me for being descended from a filthy beggar woman with no father to speak of. And they used to throw that in my face, even in Moscow. It reached them from here, thanks to Grigory Vassilyevitch. Grigory Vassilyevitch blames me for rebelling against my own birth, but I would have consented to being killed before I was ever born, rather than come into this world at all. They used to say, in the marketplace, and your own mamma too, with no delicacy whatsoever, went out of her way to tell me that her hair looked like a doormat and that she was five foot minus a tiny bit. Why say 'a tiny bit' when she could have just said 'a little bit,' like everyone else? She wanted to make it sound touching—pure peasant sentiment. Can a Russian peasant really be said to feel anything, compared to an educated man? He can't be said to have real feeling at all, given his ignorance. Ever since childhood, whenever I hear someone say 'a tiny bit,' I could burst with rage. I hate the whole of Russia, Marya Kondratyevna."
"If you'd been a cadet in the army, or a young hussar, you wouldn't talk like that—you'd have drawn your saber to defend all of Russia."
"I don't want to be a hussar, Marya Kondratyevna, and what's more, I'd like to see all soldiers abolished."
"And when an enemy comes, who's going to defend us then?"

"There's no need of defense. In 1812 there was a great invasion of Russia by Napoleon, first Emperor of the French, father of the current one, and it would have been a good thing if they'd conquered us. A clever nation would have conquered a very stupid one and annexed it. We'd have entirely different institutions now."

"Are things really so much better in their own country than they are here? I wouldn't trade one dandy I know for three young Englishmen," Marya Kondratyevna remarked tenderly, no doubt accompanying her words with a most languishing glance.
"That's a matter of preference."
"But you're just like a foreigner yourself—just like a proper, gentlemanly foreigner. I'll say it, even though it makes me blush."

"If you want to know, the folks over there and the ones here are exactly alike in their vices. They're all swindlers—it's just that over there the scoundrel wears polished boots, and here he grovels in the muck and sees nothing wrong with it. The Russian people need a good thrashing, just as Fyodor Pavlovitch said very truly yesterday, even though he's mad, and so are all his children."
"You said yourself you had such respect for Ivan Fyodorovitch."

"But he called me a stinking lackey. He thinks I might turn unruly. He's wrong about that. If I had a certain sum of money in my pocket, I'd have left this place long ago. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is lower than any lackey—in his behavior, in his mind, and in his poverty. He doesn't know how to do a single thing, and yet everyone respects him. I may be only a cook, but with a bit of luck I could open a café-restaurant on Petrovka Street in Moscow, because my cooking is something special, and there's no one in Moscow, besides the foreigners, whose cooking is anything special at all. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is a beggar, but if he challenged the son of the first count in the land, he'd fight him. Yet how exactly is he better than I am? He's far, far stupider than I am. Just look at the money he's thrown away for no reason at all!"
"A duel must be a wonderful thing," Marya Kondratyevna remarked suddenly.
"How so?"

"It must be so terrifying and so brave, especially when young officers with pistols in hand fire at each other over some lady. A perfect picture! Ah, if only girls were allowed to watch, I'd give anything to see one!"
"It's all very well when you're the one firing at someone else, but when he's firing straight at your face, you'll feel pretty foolish. You'd be glad to run away, Marya Kondratyevna."
"You don't mean to say you would run away?" But Smerdyakov didn't deign to answer. After a moment of silence, the guitar tinkled again, and he sang once more in the same falsetto:
Whatever you may say, I'm bound to go away. Life will be bright and gay In the city far away. I shall not grieve, I shall not grieve at all, I don't intend to grieve at all.

Then something unexpected happened. Alyosha suddenly sneezed. They fell silent. Alyosha got up and walked toward them. He found Smerdyakov all dressed up, wearing polished boots, his hair pomaded and perhaps even curled. The guitar lay on the garden bench. His companion was the daughter of the house, wearing a pale-blue dress with a train two yards long. She was young, and wouldn't have been bad-looking if her face hadn't been so round and so badly freckled.
"Will my brother Dmitri be back soon?" Alyosha asked, with as much composure as he could manage.
Smerdyakov got up slowly; Marya Kondratyevna rose too.
"How would I know about Dmitri Fyodorovitch? It's not as though I'm his keeper," Smerdyakov answered, quietly, distinctly, and with a hint of condescension.
"But I only asked whether you happen to know," Alyosha explained.
"I have no idea where he is, and I have no wish to know."
"But my brother told me you keep him informed of everything that goes on in the house, and that you promised to let him know when Agrafena Alexandrovna arrives."
Smerdyakov turned an unhurried, unruffled gaze on him.
"And how did you get in this time, since the gate's been bolted for an hour now?" he asked, looking at Alyosha.
"I came in from the back alley, over the fence, and went straight to the summer house. I hope you'll forgive me," he added, turning to Marya Kondratyevna. "I was in a hurry to find my brother."

"Ach, as if we'd hold it against you!" Marya Kondratyevna drawled, flattered by Alyosha's apology. "Because Dmitri Fyodorovitch often comes to the summer house that same way. We don't even know he's here, and there he is, sitting in the summer house."
"I'm very anxious to find him, or at least to learn from you where he might be now. Believe me, it's a matter of great importance to him."
"He never tells us anything," Marya Kondratyevna lisped.

"Though I used to come by here as a friend," Smerdyakov began again, "Dmitri Fyodorovitch has hounded me mercilessly, even here, with his endless questions about the master. 'Any news?' he'll ask. 'What's going on in there now? Who's coming and going?' as if I couldn't tell him something more useful. Twice already he's threatened to kill me."
"To kill you?" Alyosha exclaimed, startled.

"Do you suppose that would trouble him much, given his temper, which you had a chance to observe for yourself yesterday? He says if I let Agrafena Alexandrovna in and she spends the night there, I'll be the first one to suffer for it. I'm terribly afraid of him, and if I weren't even more afraid of doing it, I really ought to let the police know. God alone knows what he might do."
"His honor told him the other day, 'I'll grind you up in a mortar!'" Marya Kondratyevna added.
"Oh, if it's only grinding him up in a mortar, that might just be talk," Alyosha observed. "If I could meet him, I might have a word with him about that too."

"Well, the only thing I can tell you is this," said Smerdyakov, as though reconsidering, "I come here as an old friend and neighbor, so it wouldn't be strange if I didn't visit. But on the other hand, first thing this morning Ivan Fyodorovitch sent me to your brother's lodgings on Lake Street, with no letter, just a message for Dmitri Fyodorovitch to come dine with him at the restaurant here, in the marketplace. I went, but didn't find Dmitri Fyodorovitch at home, even though it was eight o'clock. 'He was here, but he's gone off entirely,' his landlady told me, in those exact words. It's almost as if there was some understanding between the two of them. Maybe at this very moment he's at the restaurant with Ivan Fyodorovitch, because Ivan Fyodorovitch hasn't been home for dinner, and Fyodor Pavlovitch dined alone an hour ago and has gone to lie down. But I beg you most particularly not to mention me, or anything I've told you, because he'd kill me over nothing at all."
"Brother Ivan invited Dmitri to the restaurant today?" Alyosha repeated quickly.
"That's right."
"The Metropolis tavern, in the marketplace?"
"The very same."
"That's quite possible," Alyosha cried, greatly excited. "Thank you, Smerdyakov, that's important. I'll go there right away."
"Don't give me away," Smerdyakov called after him.
"Oh, no, I'll go to the tavern as though I just happened by. Don't worry."
"But wait a moment, I'll open the gate for you," Marya Kondratyevna called.
"No, it's a shortcut, I'll go back over the fence."

What he'd just heard threw Alyosha into a state of great agitation. He ran to the tavern. He couldn't very well walk into the tavern in his monastic robes, but he could ask at the entrance for his brothers and call them down. But just as he reached the tavern, a window flew open, and his brother Ivan called down to him from it.
"Alyosha, can't you come up here to me? I'd be awfully grateful."
"Of course I can, only I'm not quite sure whether in this outfit—"
"But I'm in a private room. Come up the stairs; I'll run down to meet you."
A minute later Alyosha was sitting beside his brother. Ivan was dining alone.
